source.title: The Book of Business Etiquette
source.attribution: Nella Henney, The Book of Business Etiquette, Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: Public domain in the US. Nella Braddy Henney died in 1973, so the book may still be in copyright in countries using life plus 70 years.

cards.title: The real skill at work is getting things done pleasantly with other people
cards.body:
Henney points out that even a good office strains everyone's nerves. It takes real self-control to get through a hard day without striking sparks. Nobody in business works alone, she says. We are like climbers roped together on one mountain, and what each person does affects the rest.

That is why she calls the ability to work well and pleasantly with others the nearest thing to a secret of success. Talent matters, but the colleague who is skilled and easy to work with gets asked back, trusted with more and backed when things go wrong.
cards.quote: If there is a secret of success, and some of the advertisements seem trying to persuade us that it is all secret, it is the ability to work efficiently and pleasantly with other people.
cards.locator: Part I. The Book of Business Etiquette. I. The American Business Man ¶25
cards.apply_it: Think of the colleague you most enjoy working with. Name one thing they do that you could copy this week.

quiz.question: What does Henney call the nearest thing to a secret of success?
options: Having better connections than your rivals
Working longer hours than everyone else
Working efficiently and pleasantly with other people
Never showing your feelings at work
quiz.explanation: She compares people at work to climbers roped together: what each does affects all the others.

cards.title: Good manners show your character; they can't hide it
cards.body:
Henney rejects the idea of politeness as a coat of paint. She calls courtesy the Golden Rule turned into everyday conduct. It is not whitewash that covers up flaws. It is a clear varnish that shows the grain of the wood beneath.

That is both a warning and an encouragement. Smooth words with nothing behind them get found out sooner or later. But real consideration for others doesn't need polish to come across. If you want better manners at work, start with how you actually regard the people around you. The outward habits will follow.
cards.quote: It is not a white-wash which, if laid on thick enough, will cover every defect. It is a clear varnish which shows the texture and grain of the wood beneath.
cards.locator: Part I. The Book of Business Etiquette. I. The American Business Man ¶23
cards.apply_it: Pick one person you are only polite to on the surface. What would genuine consideration for them look like today?

quiz.question: What does Henney compare true courtesy to?
options: A thick coat of whitewash
A clear varnish that shows the wood beneath
A uniform everyone must wear
A mask for difficult days
quiz.explanation: Courtesy, for her, shows the character underneath rather than covering defects.

cards.title: A kind no beats a grudging yes
cards.body:
Henney quotes a leaflet a successful trust company gave its staff. Every day, people bring proposals the company has no interest in. Staff were told that these people still deserve a hearing and a courteous explanation of why the answer is no. Almost anyone can do you harm if they try, the leaflet warned, so your growth depends on the enemies you don't make as well as the friends you do.

The same goes for declining a pitch, an invitation or a job applicant today. A prompt, warm, clear no leaves people with respect for you. Saying yes through gritted teeth, or never replying at all, leaves resentment.
cards.quote: And a pleasantly expressed declination invariably makes a better impression than a favor grudgingly granted.
cards.apply_it: Is there a request sitting unanswered in your inbox? Send a short, kind no today instead of letting it go quiet.

quiz.question: According to the trust company's leaflet, what makes a better impression than a favour grudgingly granted?
options: Promising to think about it later
Ignoring the request
Passing the request to someone else
A pleasantly expressed refusal
quiz.explanation: The leaflet adds that growth depends not only on the friends you make but on the enemies you do not make.

cards.title: Marketing brings customers in, but courtesy keeps them
cards.body:
Henney tells of a bank that was losing customers and hired a publicity expert. His campaign worked at first and people came in. But they didn't stay. When he looked into it, he found they had been driven off by careless and rude service. He told the president he was wasting money on advertising while the bank treated people that way. Staff who couldn't change were let go and the rest were trained, and the trouble ended.

It is a lesson for any business today. A brilliant campaign only fills a leaky bucket faster if the experience behind it disappoints.
cards.quote: Advertising will bring in a customer but it takes courtesy to keep him.
cards.apply_it: Look at one place where customers meet your work, such as an email, a form or a phone line. Would it make them want to come back?

quiz.question: Why did the bank's advertising campaign fail at first?
options: The adverts were badly written
The bank charged too much
Customers were driven away by careless, discourteous service
Rival banks copied the campaign
quiz.explanation: People came in but did not stay; the fix was better service, not more advertising.

cards.title: One curt message can undo years of goodwill
cards.body:
Business, Henney writes, is easier to tear down than to build up, and discourtesy is one of the quickest ways to tear it down. A relationship that took years can end with one snippy letter, one cheeky answer or one rude reply on the phone.

She applies this even to chasing overdue bills. Polite, tactful reminders bring in more money than insulting ones, because a person who feels insulted decides the only way to get even is not to pay. Today the danger often sits in a hasty email or chat message. Rereading before you hit send costs seconds and can save a long relationship.
cards.quote: A contact which has taken years to build can be broken off by one snippy letter, one pert answer, or one discourteous response over the telephone.
cards.apply_it: Before sending your next tense message, read it aloud once as if you were the person receiving it.

quiz.question: What does Henney say about rude collection letters?
options: They make the debtor feel justified in not paying
They are the fastest way to get paid
They are fine once a bill is very overdue
They should be sent by phone instead
quiz.explanation: If you insult a person who owes you money, they feel the only way to get even is not to pay.

cards.title: Courtesy is a shock absorber, so use it even when you're in the right
cards.body:
Henney uses an image from a busy harbour. Tugs and ferries hang fenders over their sides because collisions are part of crowded waters. Most accidents could be softened by a fender thrown out at the right moment. At work, she says, we are all ferry boats, bumping into each other every day.

She adds a comic epitaph about William Jay, who died maintaining his right of way: he was right, dead right, but just as dead as if he'd been wrong. Most daily irritations are too small to fight over. A sense of humour and proportion settles far more of them than insisting on who is to blame.
cards.quote: Politeness is like this. It is the finest shock absorber in the world, as essential from an economic point of view as it is pleasant from a social one.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone bumps into your plans, ask: do I want to be right here, or do I want this to go smoothly?

quiz.question: What is the point of the William Jay epitaph Henney quotes?
options: Always defend your rights to the end
Traffic rules are unimportant
Accidents are always someone else's fault
Being in the right doesn't help if insisting on it wrecks you
quiz.explanation: He was 'right, dead right' but 'just as dead as if he'd been wrong'. Sometimes politeness is better than justice.

cards.title: Serve customers well, but don't grovel: business is service, not servility
cards.body:
Henney thinks the motto 'the customer is always right' is unworkable and untrue. She is especially hard on firms that put young staff on the front line with orders to accept anything. Courtesy works both ways, she says. It makes no more sense to claim the customer is always right than to claim the business always is.

Her middle path is still demanding. A good business never argues with a customer, gives them the benefit of the doubt and treats them as an intelligent adult. But it doesn't throw itself at their feet to keep their trade, however big. Serving well and keeping your self-respect go together.
cards.quote: Business is service, not servility, and courtesy works both ways.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent difficult customer or client. What would giving them the benefit of the doubt, without giving up your self-respect, have looked like?

quiz.question: What does Henney say about the motto 'the customer is always right'?
options: It is the foundation of good business
It is unworkable and untrue; business is service, not servility
It applies only to large customers
It should be posted in every shop
quiz.explanation: She still expects firms never to argue with customers and to give them the benefit of the doubt.

cards.title: Be the customer you would want to serve
cards.body:
Too little is said, Henney writes, about courtesy from customers. We talk about 'the public' with mild contempt and forget that we are the public. Its manners can be no better than the manners of the people in it.

She pictures a circus attendant answering the same silly question for the hundred-thousandth time. She also quotes a bookseller whose biggest trouble was customers who couldn't imagine the staff's side: demanding, impatient, and once phoning in the Christmas rush to ask if his wife was in the shop. Patience with people who serve you, and not asking what the sign already says, is courtesy too.
cards.quote: Each one of us speaks with more or less pitying contempt of the public, forgetting that we ourselves are the public
cards.apply_it: Next time you deal with a support line, shop or helpdesk, notice one thing you can do to make that person's job easier.

quiz.question: What did the bookshop manager call his customers' biggest failing?
options: Lack of imagination about the staff's side of things
Not buying enough books
Paying late
Complaining in writing
quiz.explanation: He said customers simply could not put themselves into the staff's place.

cards.title: The person at the top sets the tone for everyone below
cards.body:
Henney notices that a workplace usually takes on the character of the person running it. If the boss is rough and tumble, the office tends to be the same. If the boss is quiet and courteous, the office probably will be too.

She tells of a mother who was glad her son spent his first working year under a man known to be straight and decent through and through. New starters especially pick up their habits from the people above them, often without knowing it. If you lead anyone, your behaviour on a stressful day is the training they'll remember.
cards.quote: The atmosphere of most business houses is determined by the man at the top. His character filters down through the ranks.
cards.apply_it: If your team copied exactly how you behaved last week, what would you be pleased to see, and what not?

quiz.question: According to Henney, what largely determines the atmosphere of a workplace?
options: The size of the office
The company's written rules
The character of the person at the top
The age of the staff
quiz.explanation: The leader's character 'filters down through the ranks'.

cards.title: Constant surveillance breeds the rudeness it is meant to stop
cards.body:
Henney observed that workplaces with elaborate systems for spying on staff were the ones with the most rudeness and trickery. A clerk who is nagged, watched, suspected and scolded can't be expected to greet customers with a smile and a thank you.

She believed training never stops, but should be largely handed to employees themselves, and that past a certain point supervision ought to be unnecessary. She praised one trust company that had dropped its spy system while still keeping enough oversight to pin mistakes on the right person. Trust, with clear accountability, gets better behaviour than suspicion.
cards.quote: Too strict supervision--slave-driving--is fatal to courtesy.
cards.apply_it: Is there one area where you could replace checking up on someone with agreeing a clear outcome and trusting them to reach it?

quiz.question: In Henney's experience, where was rudeness and trickery most common?
options: In small family businesses
In places with elaborate systems for spying on employees
In offices with open-plan desks
In companies that paid high wages
quiz.explanation: A clerk who is 'hectored, nagged, spied upon' cannot be expected to be cheerful with customers.

cards.title: Before you punish a mistake, find out why it happened
cards.body:
Henney tells of a young clerk who made errors in figures three days running and was marked for dismissal. The employment manager talked with him first. He noticed the boy leaning forward and straining, and a red mark across his nose. The clerk had broken his glasses and couldn't afford to fix them. He said it was his problem, not the firm's.

The manager paid for the repair, and the errors stopped. A sudden dip in someone's work often has a cause you can't see from your desk. One curious, kind conversation can save a good person and a lot of trouble.
cards.quote: he discovered that the boy had broken his glasses a few days before, and that he had not had them fixed because he did not have money enough.
cards.apply_it: Is someone's work slipping lately? Ask them, privately and kindly, what's getting in the way.

quiz.question: Why was the young clerk making errors in figures?
options: He was careless and lazy
He had been badly trained
He disliked his manager
He had broken his glasses and could not afford to fix them
quiz.explanation: The manager noticed the signs, asked, paid for the repair, and the trouble stopped.

cards.title: Never criticise someone without showing them how to do better
cards.body:
Henney quotes an executive at a successful Midwestern firm with a blunt rule. If a manager found fault with a junior without explaining why, he wouldn't fire the junior. He would fire the manager. There was no room in his firm for anyone who criticised a subordinate without saying how to improve.

Criticism that only says 'that's wrong' leaves people anxious and no wiser. Feedback that names the problem, explains why it matters and points to a better way turns a mistake into learning. It also shows the person you think they can improve.
cards.quote: We have not a square inch of space in this organization for the man who criticizes a subordinate without telling him how to do better.
cards.apply_it: The next time you give critical feedback, add one concrete sentence beginning 'Next time, try...'.

quiz.question: In the executive's firm, who was fired when a manager criticised a junior without explanation?
options: The junior
Both of them
The manager
Nobody; it was only a warning
quiz.explanation: He said, 'I won't fire the boy, I fire the man.'

cards.title: Being honest doesn't oblige you to say every hurtful thing
cards.body:
'Be perfectly frank' is common advice, Henney says, but it has limits. People who pride themselves on saying exactly what they think are often just insensitive, unable to understand anyone else, and quite vain.

Her distinction is useful. You can resolve never to say anything untrue without feeling bound to say everything you think, especially when it would hurt someone's feelings or reputation. Nor should we load others with our opinions and complaints. Honesty is about not deceiving people. It isn't a licence for bluntness, and choosing what to leave unsaid is part of tact.
cards.quote: A man may determine to tell nothing but the truth, but this does not make it necessary for him to tell the whole truth, especially when it will hurt the feelings or the reputation of some one else.
cards.apply_it: Before giving a frank opinion, ask: is this true, is it needed, and is it mine to say?

quiz.question: What distinction does Henney draw about honesty?
options: You can tell only the truth without telling the whole truth when it would hurt someone
Honesty means sharing every opinion you have
White lies are always acceptable
Frankness matters more than kindness
quiz.explanation: Telling nothing but the truth doesn't require telling all of it, especially at someone else's expense.

cards.title: Dress so well that nobody notices your clothes
cards.body:
Henney's advice on dressing for work is about cleanliness and good sense, not fashion. Be clean and well groomed, and dress for your work in good, conventional clothes rather than flashy jewellery or eccentric outfits. She quotes Lord Chesterfield: dress is a foolish thing, yet it is foolish not to be well dressed.

Her test still works, whatever your gender or dress code. Good work clothes are comfortable enough that you forget them and plain enough that nobody else notices them either. That leaves attention on what you say and do. Workplace norms today are far looser than in 1922, but the test works for a suit, a uniform or a hoodie.
cards.quote: A well-dressed man is so comfortably dressed that he is not conscious of his clothes and so inconspicuously dressed that no one else is conscious of them.
cards.apply_it: Check tomorrow's outfit against two questions: will I forget I'm wearing it, and will others?

quiz.question: What is Henney's test of being well dressed for work?
options: Wearing the latest fashion
Spending as much as you can afford
Wearing something memorable
Clothes so comfortable and inconspicuous that neither you nor others notice them
quiz.explanation: Good clothes shouldn't draw attention, from you or anyone else.

cards.title: Give people physical space and keep your hands to yourself
cards.body:
Most people dislike others being too close, Henney says. Few enjoy a breath in their face, a slap on the back, a jab in the ribs or a hand on their lapel. Her safe rule is never to touch another person, because they may resent it.

She also describes salespeople who pull their chair right up to the customer's desk. One man got so tired of it that he nailed his visitor's chair to the floor, and every caller still tried to move it closer. Customs vary between people and cultures today. But leaving room and letting the other person set the distance is always the respectful default.
cards.quote: A safe rule is never to touch another person. He may resent it.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, notice the distance between you and the other person, and let them be the one to close it.

quiz.question: Why did one businessman nail his visitor's chair to the floor?
options: To stop it being stolen
Because callers kept pulling up too close to him
To make visitors uncomfortable
Because the floor was uneven
quiz.explanation: Over-eager salespeople kept hitching their chairs up close and talking into his face.

cards.title: Everyone has a right to privacy in their own head
cards.body:
Henney describes the endless questioner, like the passenger in Dickens who wanted to know the price, weight and origin of everything a stranger owned. Worse, she says, is the colleague who asks intrusive personal questions, such as someone's age or how much they earn.

Her answer is that it is perfectly fair to decline any question you don't want to answer. Open-plan offices and shared screens leave little physical privacy, which makes respecting mental privacy matter more. Let people share personal details when they choose. And it is fine to say 'I'd rather not say', politely and without apology.
cards.quote: Every man has a right to mental privacy even when he is denied, as he is in so many modern offices, any other kind of privacy.
cards.apply_it: Practise a friendly line for personal questions you'd rather not answer, such as 'Oh, I keep that one to myself.'

quiz.question: What does Henney say you may do when asked an intrusive question?
options: It is perfectly legitimate to decline to answer
You must answer to avoid seeming rude
Report the person to a manager
Answer with a joke every time
quiz.explanation: She writes that it is legitimate to refuse any question you don't wish to answer.

cards.title: Don't discuss people by name where strangers can hear
cards.body:
Henney objects to people who talk too loudly in public, whether to show off a famous name or simply through carelessness. Worst is gossip aired in lifts, on trains and in other public places. Swapping gossip is low sport, she says, and doing it out loud makes it worse.

Her rule is simple: never mention names where strangers can overhear, especially if the story is unflattering. Today that covers trains, cafés, phone calls on speaker and video calls in shared spaces. The person you are discussing may be closer than you think, and so may their friends.
cards.quote: Names should never be mentioned in a conversation in a place where strangers can overhear, especially if the connection is an unpleasant one.
cards.apply_it: Next time you take a work call in public, notice whether you're naming people. Save those details for a private room.

quiz.question: Where does Henney say names should never be mentioned?
options: In written reports
In meetings
Anywhere strangers can overhear, especially in an unpleasant connection
In conversations with your manager
quiz.explanation: Private opinions, she adds, should not be aired in public places.

cards.title: Live in your work, but also live outside it
cards.body:
Over lunch, Henney says, the talk should be real conversation that everyone at the table can share, not more shop talk. Then she widens the point. The person who can talk about only one subject is a bore, whatever the subject.

She calls it one of the saddest stories in American life: millions of people so absorbed in business that they never thought of the stars, books, trees, music or love. She pities them rather than blames them. Caring deeply about your work is good. Making sure it isn't the only thing you have is what keeps you interesting, and keeps you well.
cards.quote: It is right that a man should live in his work, but he must also live outside of it.
cards.apply_it: Name one interest that has nothing to do with your job. Give it an hour this week.

quiz.question: What does Henney say about the person of one subject?
options: They are the most successful people
They are a bore, whatever the subject
They make the best leaders
They should teach others
quiz.explanation: She thinks people should live in their work but also outside it.

cards.title: If you start a call, be there when it connects
cards.body:
Henney criticises the executive who had a secretary place a call and then wandered off, so the person on the other end had to wait while he was found. She calls this the height of discourtesy, because it says your time matters more than theirs.

The modern versions are easy to spot. You call a meeting and join five minutes late. You ring someone and put them on hold straight away. You send a meeting link and then don't turn up. Whoever asked for someone's time should be the first to arrive and ready to begin.
cards.quote: It is the acme of discourtesy to keep any one waiting in this manner. It implies that your time is much more valuable than his
cards.apply_it: For the meetings you organise this week, aim to be in the room or on the link a minute early.

quiz.question: Why does Henney call it discourteous to place a call and then wander away?
options: It wastes the phone company's money
It is against company rules
It confuses the operator
It implies your time is more valuable than the other person's
quiz.explanation: Keeping people waiting on a call you started sends the message that your time matters more.

cards.title: Picture the person on the other end, and talk as if you were face to face
cards.body:
Telephones, Henney says, are like blind people talking to each other, and people say rude, angry things over the line they would never say in person. Often they don't let the other person explain, and then slam the receiver down.

The telephone company's advice was simple: picture the person at the other end and imagine you're speaking face to face. It applies even more now, to email, chat and comments, where the other person may be no more than a name. Before you type or speak in irritation, picture the human being, probably busy and tired, who will receive it.
cards.quote: In an effort to secure better manners among their subscribers the telephone company has asked them to try to visualize the person at the other end of the wire and to imagine that they are talking face to face.
cards.apply_it: Before replying to a frustrating message, picture the sender's face and ask: would I say this to them in person?

quiz.question: What did the telephone company ask subscribers to do to improve their manners?
options: Keep calls under three minutes
Always write their complaints down instead
Visualise the person at the other end as if face to face
Speak louder
quiz.explanation: People say things over a line that they'd never say to someone's face.

cards.title: Whoever greets visitors is, for that moment, the whole company
cards.body:
Henney says millions in business are lost because firms don't value the person at the front desk. To a stranger walking in, that person is the firm. She tells of an advertising agency that lost a contract it had chased for two years. The man who came to sign it got a cheeky, offhand 'Mr Hunt isn't in' and took his business elsewhere.

Later she shows the opposite: a receptionist who greets each visitor as if they were the only one, because even 'Good morning' can be said as an insult. Today the front door is also the website chat, the support inbox and the first reply to a new enquiry.
cards.quote: To the strangers who come--and among the idlers and swindlers and beggars who assail every successful business house are potential good friends and customers--this person represents the firm,--is, for the time being, the firm itself.
cards.apply_it: Go through your organisation's front door as a stranger: the contact form, phone line or reception. What impression does it give?

quiz.question: Why did the advertising agency lose a contract it had worked on for two years?
options: The client was treated rudely at the front door
Its price was too high
The work was poor
A rival offered a bigger discount
quiz.explanation: The client was brushed off at reception and took his contract to another agency.

cards.title: Give someone your full attention, or don't agree to see them
cards.body:
Henney accepts that busy people can't see everyone who asks. But once you agree to see someone, she says, give them your full attention. It is better to refuse a meeting than to grant it grudgingly. She tells of two gruff executives who kept writing at their desks while a young visitor spoke. Years later both came to him looking for jobs, and neither got one.

She adds that a host should always ask the guest's pardon before turning to the telephone or a messenger, even when the guest is an employee. In a world of phones and laptops in meetings, that rule hasn't aged a day.
cards.quote: It is better to refuse an audience altogether than to give it grudgingly.
cards.apply_it: In your next one-to-one, put your phone face down and close your laptop. If you must check something, say so first.

quiz.question: What happened to the two executives who kept writing while their young visitor spoke?
options: They were promoted
They were never heard of again
They became his mentors
Years later they asked him for jobs and didn't get them
quiz.explanation: He knew from that first meeting what kind of people they were.

cards.title: Talk with people, not at them
cards.body:
Henney describes a nervous young salesman who rattled off a memorised speech about some charts. When he finished, the man he was visiting said he hadn't understood a word: 'You have not been talking to me. You have been talking at me.'

She says salespeople ruin themselves by sticking to a script while dodging the customer's questions. Busy people who ask a direct question want a direct answer. Good selling, like good conversation, starts from the other person's situation and responds to it. Any pitch, presentation or interview goes better when you treat the other person as a partner, not an audience.
cards.quote: 'You have not been talking to me,' he explained. 'You have been talking at me.'
cards.apply_it: In your next pitch or presentation, stop after two minutes and ask a real question about the other person's situation.

quiz.question: What mistake did Henney say ruins many young salespeople?
options: Asking too many questions
Sticking to a prepared script and passing over the customer's questions
Dressing too formally
Talking too slowly
quiz.explanation: When a buyer asks a direct question, they want a direct answer.

cards.title: Sell things that won't come back to customers who will
cards.body:
For Henney, salesmanship is service. Anyone who talks someone into buying what they don't want, don't need and can't use is, in her word, a scoundrel. She quotes a motto: good selling means selling goods that won't come back to customers that will.

She warns against overselling too, like the share salesmen who urged people to mortgage their homes to buy more. A pushy sale may work while the seller is in the room, but discontent follows. A satisfied customer still happy a year later tells friends, and soon the product almost sells itself.
cards.quote: 'Good salesmanship,' and this is the only sort that any self-respecting man will engage in, 'is selling goods that won't come back to customers that will.'
cards.apply_it: Before your next sale or recommendation, ask: will this person still be glad they said yes a year from now?

quiz.question: According to Henney's motto, what is good salesmanship?
options: Selling goods that won't come back to customers that will
Closing as many deals as possible today
Persuading people to buy more than they planned
Always offering the cheapest option
quiz.explanation: Lasting business comes from satisfied customers who return and recommend you.

cards.title: Treat everyone with the same respect, whatever their rank
cards.body:
A good salesman, Henney says, is courteous to all people alike: overalls get as much respect as fine broadcloth. It pays in money, she adds, and in things worth more.

Later she turns this on office life. She describes the employee who feels hurt that the president doesn't say good morning in the hall, yet won't say good morning to the person who brings his post or good night to the cleaner. Her advice is to worry about no one's behaviour but your own. How you treat people who can do nothing for you shows your manners more clearly than anything else.
cards.quote: And a good salesman is courteous to all men alike. With him overalls command as much respect as broadcloth.
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow, greet by name someone at work you usually walk past: a cleaner, a guard, a receptionist.

quiz.question: What does Henney mean by 'overalls command as much respect as broadcloth'?
options: Workers should dress better
Expensive cloth is a better investment
A good salesperson respects everyone equally, whatever their status
Salespeople should dress casually
quiz.explanation: Courtesy shouldn't depend on how important someone seems.

cards.title: Build up your own business instead of running down your rivals
cards.body:
Henney follows a salesman who meets a prospect loyal to a rival supplier, Hicks and Hicks. Instead of attacking them, he agrees they are a good firm and there's no reason to leave them. He simply asks to be remembered if they ever run short.

She thinks that was wise. He left goodwill, and if the rival ever had a strike, a fire or a closure, the customer would turn to him. Elsewhere she advises an honest word of praise for competitors where it's deserved, and silence where it isn't. Knocking rivals makes you look afraid of them.
cards.quote: This salesman never forgets that his part of the job is to build up business for his own firm, and not to tear down business for other firms.
cards.locator: A While with a Traveling Man ¶31
cards.apply_it: Next time a client mentions a competitor, find one fair thing to say about them, then talk about what you do well.

quiz.question: How did the salesman respond when the prospect said he bought from Hicks and Hicks?
options: He listed their faults
He praised them as reliable and asked to be remembered if they fell short
He offered a steep discount
He ended the meeting at once
quiz.explanation: He built goodwill for his own firm without tearing down another's.

cards.title: Every message has two jobs: get the point across and build goodwill
cards.body:
Henney says half of all business letters should never be written, and many of the rest are so muddled that a matter needing two letters takes six or eight. Rules of thumb are risky, she says, but two things are essential. A letter must get its idea across, and it must build goodwill. The best letter does both most courteously and most completely in the shortest space.

Those tests suit email and chat perfectly. Before sending, ask whether the reader will understand exactly what you mean and what you need, and whether they'll feel well treated. If either answer is no, rewrite.
cards.quote: The letter must succeed in getting its idea across and it must build up good will for its firm.
cards.apply_it: Take your next important email and check it against both tests: is it clear, and is it kind?

quiz.question: What two things does Henney say every business letter must do?
options: Be long and detailed
Mention the price and the deadline
Use formal phrases and a printed letterhead
Get its idea across and build goodwill
quiz.explanation: And the best letter does both most courteously in the briefest space.

cards.title: Cut the stiff phrases and write the way you'd speak
cards.body:
Henney lists stock phrases of 1920s business letters: 'Replying to your esteemed favor', 'contents noted', 'We beg to remain'. She calls them dead weight. Legal wording belongs in contracts, not ordinary letters. She contrasts a stiff note from a furniture firm with a plain version that says the same thing in half the words and sounds far friendlier.

The phrases have changed, but the habit hasn't. 'Per my last email', 'please be advised' and 'kindly revert' are today's equivalents. Plain, conversational language is clearer, quicker to read and warmer.
cards.quote: It is perfectly possible to express oneself clearly in the language of conversation (which is also the language of business) without burying the meaning in tiresome verbiage.
cards.apply_it: Scan your last three sent emails for a stock phrase you'd never say out loud, and retire it.

quiz.question: What does Henney say about phrases like 'We beg to remain'?
options: They show proper respect
They are required in formal letters
They are dead weight that should be stripped out
They should be used only with new customers
quiz.explanation: She says you can write clearly in the language of conversation, which is also the language of business.

cards.title: Answer the question that was actually asked
cards.body:
Standard replies save time, Henney admits, but there's no excuse for sending one that doesn't answer the question. She tells of a woman new to New York who lost her key and wrote to her landlord. He replied curtly that replacing keys was 'up to them'. She had meant to pay all along. All she needed was a locksmith's address or a key with a small charge added.

A reply like that is only efficient for the sender. Read the message as the person who wrote it: what do they need, and what would help them next? Then answer that, even if it takes one extra line.
cards.quote: The man who is answering a letter must put himself in the place of the one who wrote it.
cards.apply_it: Before sending your next reply, reread the original message and check you've answered what was actually asked.

quiz.question: What would have been a better reply from the landlord?
options: A short apology plus a locksmith's address, or the key with a small charge
A curt note that keys are the tenant's problem
No reply at all
A long explanation of the cost of keys
quiz.explanation: Henney gives both of those alternatives. Each takes no more effort than the curt reply.

cards.title: Don't thank people in advance for favours they haven't agreed to
cards.body:
Henney thinks it goes too far to send thanks in advance for a favour you expect someone to do. Even people who like doing favours want to feel they chose to. If you take a yes for granted, you take away the pleasure of giving it. Only royalty, she says, can simply state its wishes and expect them done, and royalty has gone out of fashion.

The modern 'Thanks in advance!' at the end of an email can have the same effect. Ask clearly, make it easy to say no, and save your thanks for when they have actually helped.
cards.quote: Even those who take pleasure in granting favors like to feel that they do so of their own free will.
cards.apply_it: In your next request, swap 'Thanks in advance' for 'Would you be able to...?' and thank them properly afterwards.

quiz.question: Why does Henney object to thanking people in advance for a favour?
options: It wastes words
It makes the request sound urgent
It is too informal
It assumes the favour is done and removes the sense of free choice
quiz.explanation: People like to feel they grant favours of their own free will.

cards.title: Write the angry message if you must, but don't send it
cards.body:
Henney's rule is simple: never write a letter while you're angry. If you do write one, and sometimes it's a relief, don't post it. She tells a story about Theodore Roosevelt. He would dictate furious letters to people who deserved them, and his secretary would quietly hold them back. Next day Roosevelt would ask if the letter had gone. On hearing it hadn't, he'd say, 'Good! We won't send it!'

Today's 'send' button works faster than any secretary. Write the angry draft in a notes app, not your email, then come back once you've cooled down.
cards.quote: No one should write a letter while he is angry, or if he writes it (and it is sometimes a relief to write a scorching letter) he should not mail it.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're furious about a message, write your reply somewhere it can't be sent, and reread it tomorrow.

quiz.question: What did Roosevelt usually say when told his angry letter had not been sent?
options: 'Send it now!'
'Good! We won't send it!'
'Write a stronger one.'
'Who stopped it?'
quiz.explanation: His secretary held the letters back, and after cooling down he was always glad they had not gone.

cards.title: Write references that are honest as well as generous
cards.body:
Nobody, Henney says, should recommend a person for qualities they know that person doesn't have. Be as favourable as you honestly can, and state any reservations plainly.

She tells of a committee that wanted to replace General Gorgas, the man in charge of cleaning up Panama. Roosevelt asked a respected doctor for an opinion of their candidate. The doctor praised him highly but said he wouldn't be as good as the man already there. Roosevelt kept Gorgas, and events proved him right. 'Would to heaven,' he said, 'that every one would write such honest letters of recommendation!'
cards.quote: No man should allow himself to recommend another for qualities which he knows he does not possess.
cards.apply_it: Next time you write a reference, list three specific strengths you've seen, and leave out anything you can't stand behind.

quiz.question: Why did Roosevelt value the doctor's letter?
options: It praised the candidate honestly but said the current man was better
It was very short
It recommended nobody
It was written by a famous author
quiz.explanation: Honest references are worth more because they can be trusted.

cards.title: Acknowledge complaints straight away and take every one seriously
cards.body:
Henney's rule is to acknowledge complaints immediately. If you need time to look into it, say so and ask for patience. Every complaint deserves careful, courteous attention, she says, because most are justified, and even the ones that aren't started from something real.

She has advice for complainers too. Don't write in haste or anger. Say plainly what happened, when and how, and don't blame an individual for what may have been bad luck. 'Please', she says, goes further than 'Now, see here'. Quick, calm handling on both sides turns most complaints into fixable problems.
cards.quote: Most of them are justified, and even those that are not had something to begin on.
cards.apply_it: If you have a complaint waiting, send a quick 'We've got this and are looking into it' today, even before you have the answer.

quiz.question: What does Henney say about complaints that turn out not to be justified?
options: They should be ignored
They should be answered sharply
Even they had something real to begin with
They prove the customer is dishonest
quiz.explanation: She asks for careful, courteous attention to every complaint.

cards.title: Polite words can't make up for unsafe conditions or unfair pay
cards.body:
Henney tells a true story of a factory with polished, courteous offices at the front. At the back, hundreds of workers rode a rusty, rotten lift that had already had three serious accidents. The management knew and did nothing. She says that kind of politeness is polish laid over something rotten, and it isn't courtesy at all.

She says the same about pay. Bosses who are kind in the corridor but pay less than a living wage show a politeness, she writes, not worth a tinker's curse. Justice comes first: safety, decent conditions, fair pay. Courtesy only counts on top of those.
cards.quote: but polish laid over a cancerous growth like this is not courtesy.
cards.apply_it: If you manage people, list one thing about their pay, safety or conditions you've been meaning to fix, and take a first step this week.

quiz.question: Why does Henney say the factory's courteous management was not truly courteous?
options: Its offices were untidy
It ignored a dangerous lift its workers had to use
It paid its executives too much
It had no reception desk
quiz.explanation: She writes that courtesy cannot cover a failure of basic justice and care.

cards.title: Treat your start time as an appointment you've promised to keep
cards.body:
Henney notes that most people are paid to be at work at a set hour. In effect they have a daily appointment with their job, and keeping it is wise and honourable. Lateness is a habit, she says, and like most habits it's easier to form than to break. Punctuality is a habit too, harder to build because it rests on strength rather than weakness.

The same goes for any time you've agreed: a shift, a meeting, a deadline. Being reliably on time is one of the simplest ways to show people they can count on you.
cards.quote: They have a daily appointment with their business at a specified time. It is wise and honorable to keep it.
cards.apply_it: Pick the commitment you're most often late for and set a reminder ten minutes earlier for the next week.

quiz.question: How does Henney describe the agreed start time of work?
options: As a rough guideline
As less important than the quality of work
As something only managers need to keep
As a daily appointment that is honourable to keep
quiz.explanation: She also notes that lateness, like punctuality, is a habit.

cards.title: Don't go over your manager's head without telling them first
cards.body:
Henney sets out a rule for anyone with a grievance or a good idea. Raise it first with your immediate manager. If that fails, you may take it higher, but never without letting them know. She says the same applies to suggestions: take them to your own boss first.

She adds two honest observations. If you're always clashing with your manager, it may be better to find another job. And if you find you're in trouble with every boss you have, the fault probably isn't all theirs. Going around someone in secret damages trust far more than an open disagreement does.
cards.quote: He should never, unless the circumstances are unusual, go over his head and he should never do so without letting him know.
cards.apply_it: If you're thinking of escalating something, first tell your manager plainly: 'I'd like to take this to X, and I wanted you to know.'

quiz.question: What does Henney say about going over your immediate superior's head?
options: It is never allowed
It is fine whenever you disagree
Only in unusual cases, and never without telling them
Only if a customer asks you to
quiz.explanation: Openness keeps trust even when you disagree.

cards.title: Never pass the blame down to someone below you
cards.body:
'Passing the buck' is very tempting, Henney admits: shifting blame for a mistake onto the person one step below. But she points out that the buck always passes down, never up. That makes it worse, because it lands on people least able to defend themselves.

She recalls the old knightly duty to protect the weak. Anyone who blames someone else for their own fault, or lets them take the blame, she calls beneath contempt. If you lead people, owning the mistake publicly and sorting out the details privately is how you earn their loyalty.
cards.quote: The 'buck,' as has been pointed out, always passes down and not up, a fact which makes a detestable practice all the more odious.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent mistake on your team. Have you clearly owned your share of it? If not, say so.

quiz.question: Why does Henney think 'passing the buck' is especially bad?
options: It always passes down to those less able to defend themselves
It wastes time
It confuses the accounts
It annoys customers
quiz.explanation: Blame shifted downward lands on the weakest, which she calls beneath contempt.

cards.title: Correct people quietly and in private
cards.body:
When a mistake has been traced to the right person, Henney says, any reprimand should be quiet. Good managers don't shout their reproofs, and they don't need to. A rebuke is between the person and their boss. Nobody else needs to hear it, and there's no reason to feed office gossip.

Public telling-off humiliates the person, makes everyone watching uneasy, and turns a learning moment into a story that goes round the building. A calm, private word fixes the problem and leaves the person's dignity whole.
cards.quote: Good managers do not shout their reprimands. They do not need to. The reproof for a fault is a matter between the offender and the 'boss.'
cards.apply_it: If you need to correct someone this week, book a private moment and use a calm, even voice.

quiz.question: According to Henney, how should good managers reprimand someone?
options: Loudly, so others learn from it
In writing to the whole team
Not at all
Quietly, as a private matter between the two of them
quiz.explanation: No one else has any concern with it, and there is no reason to feed gossip.

cards.title: When you leave a job, leave with dignity
cards.body:
Whether you resign or are let go, Henney says, your departure should be pleasant, or at least dignified. It is childish to use your last days to tell everyone you have a grudge against what you think of them. Running down the employer that let you go is worse than bad manners.

If the firm wronged someone else, speak up about that. On your own behalf, keep quiet. Even if the fault was all theirs, calling names doesn't help. Self-respect is the best guide here. Your old colleagues, references and reputation will follow you to the next job.
cards.quote: It is childish to take advantage of the fact that you are going away to tell all of the people you have grudges against how you feel about them
cards.apply_it: If you ever leave a job, plan your goodbye message in advance and keep it to thanks and good wishes.

quiz.question: What does Henney advise about speaking out when you leave a job?
options: Air every grudge, since you have nothing to lose
Stay silent on your own account, though you may speak up for others wronged
Write a public review immediately
Never speak to former colleagues again
quiz.explanation: She calls this the time when it is right to be 'too proud to fight'.

cards.title: Ask your team, don't order them, and respect their own time
cards.body:
Henney describes a good manager working with an assistant. He doesn't make a habit of eating into her lunch hour or keeping her a few minutes after closing. When there's a real reason to stay late, he asks courteously whether she would mind. If she has a good reason to go, she says so briefly.

He asks her to do whatever needs doing, but with a 'Please' and a 'Thank you', not a 'See here'. Elsewhere Henney says employers who regularly keep staff past closing time are as rude as clock-watchers. Asking, not assuming, keeps goodwill for the days when you really need the extra effort.
cards.quote: he does it with a 'Please' and a 'Thank you,' and not with a 'See, here' and a 'Say, listen to me, now.'
cards.apply_it: Next time you need someone to stay late or pick up extra work, ask, explain why, and mean it if they say no.

quiz.question: How does the good manager in Henney's example handle asking his assistant to stay late?
options: He asks courteously, and only when there is a real reason
He expects it without asking
He never asks under any circumstances
He offers a bonus every time
quiz.explanation: He doesn't make overtime a habit, and he asks with a 'Please' and a 'Thank you'.

cards.title: Learn to stay calm when a stressed boss is unfair
cards.body:
Henney imagines an office boy summoned by a harassed, overloaded manager who snaps that he rang half an hour ago, when it was really two minutes. Should the boy correct him? Not if he values his job, she says. The outburst is unjust and indefensible, and the manager wouldn't defend it the next day. But staying calm in the face of injustice is one of the first lessons of discipline.

She isn't asking anyone to accept mistreatment. If there's an opening later, you can calmly explain what happened. The point is not to get into a shouting match with someone who is plainly overwhelmed.
cards.quote: Of course it is unjust, but one of the first laws of discipline is to learn to be composed in the face of injustice
cards.apply_it: Next time someone snaps at you unfairly under pressure, take a breath, don't argue in the moment, and raise it calmly later if it still matters.

quiz.question: What does Henney advise when a stressed boss is unfair in the moment?
options: Argue back immediately
Report them at once
Stay composed and explain later if there is an opening
Quit on the spot
quiz.explanation: If an explanation turns into a shouting match, she says it is best to stay silent.

cards.title: When you ask for five minutes, stop at five
cards.body:
Henney follows a salesman who keeps calling on a famously 'hard customer'. He finally gets in by writing on his card that he wants only five minutes. He plunges straight in, talks entirely in terms of the customer's business, and when his time is up he says so himself and offers to come back another day.

The customer tells him to stay and fires questions at him. Half an hour later the salesman leaves with the order and a new friend. Keeping your word about time, even when it's going well, shows people you can be trusted with more of it.
cards.quote: 'I'm sorry,' he says, 'but my five minutes are up. Will you let me come back some day when you are not so busy and tell you more about it?'
cards.locator: A While with a Traveling Man ¶21
cards.apply_it: In your next short meeting, watch the clock and offer to stop on time, even if things are going well.

quiz.question: What happened when the salesman pointed out that his five minutes were up?
options: He was shown the door
The customer told him to stay and began asking questions
He was asked to come back next year
He was told to send a letter instead
quiz.explanation: Keeping his promise about time earned him more time and the order.

cards.title: On a journey, be as comfortable as you like, but not at others' expense
cards.body:
Henney's travel advice is mostly about sharing a small space. Carry little luggage, since piles of bags cramp everyone. Don't sprawl over seats or wander up and down the carriage. Don't chat loudly across the sleeping car. If others object to an open window, it stays shut.

On talking to strangers, she says conversation should only start if it comes naturally. Many people work while travelling, and it is fair for them to turn an intrusive talker away. Never push yourself on anyone. On a plane, train or shared office, the same idea applies: your comfort ends where someone else's begins.
cards.quote: A traveler may make himself as comfortable as he likes so long as it is not at the expense of the other passengers.
cards.apply_it: On your next journey, check your space: bags, volume, elbows, screen brightness. Would the person beside you be happy with it?

quiz.question: What does Henney say about starting conversations with strangers when travelling?
options: Always introduce yourself to everyone nearby
Only if you plan to sell them something
Never speak to strangers at all
Only when it comes about naturally, and never force yourself on anyone
quiz.explanation: Many people work while travelling, so it is within courtesy to turn aside an intrusive talker.

cards.title: A great host guides you so smoothly you don't notice
cards.body:
Henney describes a young banker on his first trip to New York, lost in front of a menu and a row of forks. His experienced host doesn't lecture him. He suggests dishes, mentions what is good that season and quietly guides the meal, so the young man thinks he is managing it all himself.

She holds up a scene from Dickens too. Herbert Pocket teaches Pip city table manners so lightly that they both laugh and Pip barely blushes. Real courtesy, she says, is not just being at ease yourself but putting the other person at ease. That goes for hosting a client, welcoming a new hire or showing someone round.
cards.quote: Throughout the meal the host makes comments and suggestions and guides his guest through to the end, and does it so graciously that the young man from Smithville is not aware that he is doing it, and feels that it is all due to his own quick observation that he is getting along so well.
cards.apply_it: Next time you host someone in unfamiliar surroundings, offer one gentle suggestion before they have to ask.

quiz.question: What makes the city host 'perfect' in Henney's story?
options: He orders the most expensive dishes
He corrects his guest's mistakes openly
He guides his guest so gracefully the guest doesn't notice
He lets the guest work everything out alone
quiz.explanation: The guest feels he is doing well by his own observation. That is the mark of a perfect host.

cards.title: Thank people for every small kindness
cards.body:
Henney notices that when someone gives up a seat on a crowded tram, the person who takes it often sits down without even a glance, as if the act weren't worth noticing. Rudeness, she says, is shared fairly evenly between men and women. And a small kindness often costs a tired person more than it seems.

Her rule is short. Every act of civility or thoughtfulness deserves at least a 'Thank you', and a warm one. It applies to the colleague who holds a door, covers a shift or answers a quick question. Noticing and thanking people makes them much more likely to keep being kind.
cards.quote: Every act of civility or thoughtfulness should be rewarded with at least a 'Thank you' and a good hearty one at that.
cards.apply_it: Today, thank three people out loud for small things you might normally let pass.

quiz.question: What does Henney say every act of civility deserves?
options: At least a hearty 'Thank you'
A gift in return
Nothing, since courtesy is expected
A written note
quiz.explanation: She notes that many people accept kindness without a glance, which discourages it.

cards.title: Be courteous to your work itself by doing it well
cards.body:
In her last chapter Henney names what she thinks may be the most valuable courtesy in business: politeness towards your own job. Looking well and being pleasant matter, but at work the main concern should be the work, not yourself. The point of business is getting things done, she says, and courtesy matters because it makes getting things done easier and more pleasant.

She ends with Kipling: the wisest thing a person can do is the work under their nose, with the tools under their hand. Good manners and good work aren't separate. Doing your job carefully is a form of respect for everyone who depends on it.
cards.quote: We have said a good deal as we came along about courtesy toward oneself and other people, but perhaps the most valuable of all courtesies in business is politeness toward one's job.
cards.apply_it: Pick one task you've been doing on autopilot and give it your full care today.

quiz.question: What does Henney call perhaps the most valuable courtesy in business?
options: Politeness toward customers
Politeness toward rivals
Politeness toward the boss
Politeness toward one's job
quiz.explanation: Courtesy is valuable because it makes getting things done easy and pleasant, and the work comes first.
